description: Reasoning vault for quadratic equations aligned with OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5: factoring and the zero product property, square root property (over R and C), completing the square, quadratic formula, discriminant classification, derivation flaw diagnosis, and constrained quadratic modeling.

archetypes.name: Solving Monic Quadratic Equations by Factoring and Zero Product Property
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — Solving Quadratic Equations by Factoring
archetypes.coreConcept: Rewrite a monic quadratic equation as x^2 + bx + c = 0, factor into (x - r_1)(x - r_2) = 0 (or factor out x when c = 0), and apply the Zero Product Property so each linear factor equals zero.
archetypes.mentalModel: A product equals zero if and only if at least one factor equals zero; factoring breaks a degree-2 equation into degree-1 equations.
archetypes.governingRelation: x^2 + bx + c = (x - r_1)(x - r_2) = 0 \implies x = r_1 \lor x = r_2

cognitiveTraps.description: Reading the constant signs inside the factored binomials (x + p)(x + q) = 0 directly as the roots x = p, q instead of solving x + p = 0 to get x = -p.
Dividing both sides of x^2 + bx = 0 by x and losing the root x = 0.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Solving Quadratic Equations via the Square Root Property
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — Solving Quadratics by the Square Root Property
archetypes.coreConcept: Isolate the squared expression u^2 = k (where u = x - h) before taking square roots of both sides to get u = ±sqrt(k), yielding two real roots when k > 0 or complex conjugate roots when k < 0.
archetypes.mentalModel: Squaring erases sign, so undoing a square must restore both positive and negative branches around the shift h.
archetypes.governingRelation: a(x - h)^2 = c \implies (x - h)^2 = \frac{c}{a} \implies x = h \pm \sqrt{\frac{c}{a}}

cognitiveTraps.description: Taking only the principal positive square root and discarding the negative branch.
Taking the square root of a*x^2 = c as a*x = ±sqrt(c) instead of dividing by a before taking the root.
Treating sqrt(-n) as sqrt(n) or declaring no algebraic root when asked for complex solutions.
cognitiveTraps.trapFormula: x = h \pm \sqrt{|k|} \text{ instead of } h \pm i\sqrt{|k|}

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Rearranging and Factoring Non-Monic Quadratic Equations
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — Solving Quadratic Equations by Factoring
archetypes.coreConcept: Move all terms to one side so the right-hand side is strictly 0, remove any common numerical factor, and factor ax^2 + bx + c = 0 by AC-splitting/grouping before applying the Zero Product Property.
archetypes.mentalModel: The Zero Product Property holds exclusively for 0; setting a product equal to any non-zero constant k gives infinitely many factor pairs.
archetypes.governingRelation: ax^2 + bx + c = d \implies ax^2 + bx + (c - d) = 0

cognitiveTraps.description: Factoring the left-hand side equal to a nonzero constant k and setting each linear factor equal to k.
cognitiveTraps.trapFormula: (x - p)(x - q) = k \implies x - p = k \lor x - q = k

cognitiveTraps.description: Finding two integers m, n with m*n = a*c and m + n = b and writing (x + m)(x + n) = 0 without dividing back by a or grouping.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Solving Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — Completing the Square
archetypes.coreConcept: Move the constant term to the right, divide every term by the leading coefficient a when a != 1, add (b/(2a))^2 to both sides to form a perfect-square trinomial (x + b/(2a))^2, and apply the square root property.
archetypes.mentalModel: Reshaping x^2 + px into a geometric square of side (x + p/2) requires adding the corner piece (p/2)^2 to both sides of the balance.

cognitiveTraps.description: Adding (p/2)^2 to the left side to complete the square while leaving the right side unchanged.
Adding p^2 instead of (p/2)^2 when completing the square on x^2 + px.
Adding (b/2)^2 to ax^2 + bx = -c without dividing the equation by a first.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Solving Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — Using the Quadratic Formula
archetypes.coreConcept: Put the equation into standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, read signed coefficients a, b, c carefully, and compute x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a), simplifying radicals and extracting i when the discriminant is negative.
archetypes.mentalModel: The quadratic formula packages completing the square once and for all, separating the axis of symmetry (-b/(2a)) from the symmetric offset (±sqrt(Δ)/(2a)).

cognitiveTraps.description: Writing +b instead of -b in the numerator of the quadratic formula.
Dividing the numerator by 2 instead of 2a when the leading coefficient a != 1.
Computing b^2 + 4ac instead of b^2 - 4ac inside the radical.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Root Classification and Threshold Analysis via the Discriminant
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — The Discriminant
archetypes.coreConcept: Evaluate Δ = b^2 - 4ac on standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 to determine whether the equation has two distinct real solutions (Δ > 0), one repeated real solution (Δ = 0), or two non-real complex conjugate solutions (Δ < 0), and solve for unknown coefficient thresholds.
archetypes.mentalModel: The discriminant sits inside the square root and determines whether the symmetric offset from the vertex -b/(2a) is real positive, zero, or purely imaginary.
archetypes.governingRelation: \Delta = b^2 - 4ac \;\begin{cases} > 0 & \text{two distinct real roots} \\ = 0 & \text{one repeated real root} \\ < 0 & \text{two complex conjugate roots} \end{cases}

cognitiveTraps.description: Evaluating (-|b|)^2 as -|b|^2 instead of +|b|^2 when b is negative.
Dropping the double negative in -4ac when a > 0 and c < 0, subtracting 4a|c| instead of adding it.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Diagnosing Algebraic Flaws in Quadratic Equation Derivations
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 (beyond-the-book diagnostic extension)
archetypes.coreConcept: Inspect a line-by-line solution of a quadratic equation and locate the exact line where algebraic equivalence breaks (Zero Product Property on nonzero RHS, unbalanced completing the square, dropped ± branch, or wrong formula denominator). L3 diagnose form: prompt shows 'Line N: $...$' lines and asks which line is the first wrong line (answerSpec choice with verify.flaw).
archetypes.mentalModel: Every valid transformation preserves the solution set; the first flawed line alters either the algebraic value or the solution set.

cognitiveTraps.description: Applying factor-equals-RHS when the right-hand side is nonzero.
cognitiveTraps.trapFormula: (x - p)(x - q) = k \implies x - p = k

cognitiveTraps.description: Failing to notice that completing the square added a constant to only the left side.
Overlooking denominator 2 instead of 2a in the quadratic formula step.
Missing the dropped ± sign when taking the square root of both sides.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Constrained Quadratic Modeling and Domain Filtering
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 — Applications of Quadratic Equations
archetypes.coreConcept: Combine two geometric, kinematic, or financial/rate relationships from a situation into a single quadratic equation, select an appropriate solving method, and filter out roots that violate physical bounds (negative lengths, times before release, or frame widths exceeding container dimensions).
archetypes.mentalModel: Algebraic equations know nothing about physical positivity or geometric bounds; solving yields candidate roots that must be vetted against the domain.
archetypes.governingRelation: f(x) = g(x) \implies ax^2 + bx + c = 0,\quad x \in D_{\text{valid}}

cognitiveTraps.description: Reporting a mathematically valid root that violates geometric or physical constraints (such as negative length or width larger than half the outer span).
Adding uniform border width w once (L + w)(W + w) instead of twice (L + 2w)(W + 2w) around all four sides.
Dropping one root before checking which root satisfies the physical question (e.g., earlier vs. later height crossing).

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.

archetypes.name: Parameter Synthesis from Discriminant Feasibility and Root Relations
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §2.5 (beyond-the-book synthesis extension)
archetypes.coreConcept: Determine an unknown coefficient parameter in a quadratic equation by coupling a root-structure relation (such as repeated root Δ = 0, difference/sum/product of roots via Vieta's formulas, or a given ratio of roots) with the discriminant feasibility condition and rejecting parameter branches that violate realness or positivity.
archetypes.mentalModel: Root conditions produce a quadratic (or algebraic) constraint on the parameter itself; every candidate parameter must be checked back against Δ and any side conditions.

cognitiveTraps.description: Accepting a parameter candidate that satisfies the algebraic root relation without checking the sign or discriminant bound required by the problem.
Using r_1 + r_2 = +b/a instead of -b/a when relating coefficients to roots.
Writing -b^2 instead of +b^2 in the discriminant constraint for the parameter.

archetypes.figureNone: Quadratic equations solved algebraically; a parabola graph would show the roots.
